# Richard Stallman Summary
Richard Stallman, born in 1953 in New York City, is a prominent figure in the history of computing and the free software movement. As a Harvard student, he became a programmer at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and contributed to major software projects like TECO and Emacs. Stallman published a foundational paper on AI truth maintenance systems and was known for his opposition to restricted computer access. He became a leading voice against proprietary software, advocating for user freedom to modify and share programs. In 1984, Stallman left MIT to work full-time on the GNU project, aiming to create a free operating system compatible with Unix. He founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF) in 1985 and introduced key concepts such as copyleft and the GNU General Public License (GPL), instrumental to the growth of free software.
Stallman contributed several core GNU tools (Emacs, GCC, GDB), but the GNU project lacked a kernel until the Linux kernel was created using GNU development tools in 1991, leading to the formation of GNU/Linux. He is known for his uncompromising advocacy for free software and insistence on precise terminology, rejecting "open-source" in favor of "free software." Stallman has actively campaigned against digital rights management (DRM), software patents, and proprietary software, and has advanced ideas for copyright reduction. He has promoted surveillance resistance and privacy, refusing to use non-free software and advocating for secure, free digital practices. Stallman has received numerous honors and published influential works, but his career has also been marked by controversy, including his resignation from MIT and the FSF in 2019 following public backlash over comments on sensitive topics; he was later reinstated to the FSF board in 2021.
